name: Yohimbine

lead: Yohimbine comes from yohimbe bark and blocks alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, which increases noradrenaline activity. It is a common ingredient in pre-workouts and fat burners.

Cutting forums use it for stubborn fat, often with caffeine and fasted cardio. The studies found here are small topical-fat trials and research uses of the drug as a stress probe; none shows oral fat loss in dieting men.

paras: By blocking presynaptic alpha-2 receptors it raises norepinephrine release, which proponents say promotes lipolysis in fat depots that resist it. The effect is short-lived, with a half-life reported as under about an hour.

Documented adverse effects include anxiety, high blood pressure, fast heart rate and gastrointestinal upset, with rare severe cases. It requires a prescription in some countries and is sold as a supplement in others.

lead: Yohimbine is an indole alkaloid obtained from the bark of the African tree Pausinystalia yohimbe. It acts as a selective antagonist of alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, which raises norepinephrine release and sympathetic activity [1][2]. It has been used in folk medicine as an aphrodisiac, and prescription yohimbine hydrochloride has been studied for erectile dysfunction [1][3].

In bodybuilding and cutting circles it is promoted as a fat-loss supplement, particularly for "stubborn" fat and for use with fasted cardio. The reasoning is that alpha-2 receptors in some fat depots resist lipolysis and yohimbine blocks them [4][5][6]. It is an ingredient in many pre-workout and fat-burner products [7][8].

Published evidence on fat loss is thin. A 1995 set of small trials tested topical yohimbine-containing preparations on women's thigh fat [4]. Reviews of erectile dysfunction treatments and natural aphrodisiacs discuss it as a candidate [9][10]. Known adverse effects include anxiety, raised blood pressure and heart rate, and gastrointestinal upset [1].

paras: Yohimbine blocks alpha-2 adrenoceptors, including presynaptic autoreceptors that normally limit noradrenaline release, so it increases noradrenergic signalling [2][1]. Researchers use it as an experimental way to provoke noradrenergic and stress responses in humans and animals, for example in studies of anxiety, decision making and drug cue reactivity [11][12][13][14]. It also increases salivary secretion in humans [15]. Grokipedia reports a short half-life of roughly 0.5 to 1 hour [1].

On looksmax.org, a thread titled as a "legit or cope" question asks whether yohimbine helps already-lean users reach single-digit body fat. Replies say it is in their pre-workout, that it makes fasted cardio more effective, and that excess makes users feel sick [5]. On T Nation, users list it in cutting stacks with caffeine, carnitine, ephedra-type stimulants and cardarine [16][6][17]. Reports describe strong stimulant effects including tingling, chills and a runny nose [18][19]. These are individual accounts; no dose guidance is given here.

A 1995 report described three small trials in overweight women using one thigh as a double-blind control, including an ointment containing forskolin, yohimbine and aminophylline applied to the thigh alongside diet and walking [4]. The abstract available here does not allow a summary of the effect size.

Other human studies use yohimbine as a research tool rather than a treatment: effects on action monitoring [12], approach-avoidance behaviour with hydrocortisone [11], pain perception [20], and drug cue reactivity [13]. A bioequivalence study of 5 mg tablets was registered in erectile dysfunction [3], and a trial in type 2 diabetes patients with a genetic variant was also registered [21]. A systematic review of supplements in elite soccer players is listed in the literature, but its abstract does not report yohimbine findings [22]. No trial located here has tested oral yohimbine for fat loss or physique change in healthy dieting men.

Reported adverse effects include anxiety, hypertension, tachycardia and gastrointestinal distress, with rare severe toxicity such as seizures and myocardial infarction reported at high doses [1]. A case report describes yohimbine-induced bronchospasm [23], and a review of herb-drug interactions lists it among herbal products with interaction potential [24]. Product labels and regulators advise caution in people with cardiovascular or psychiatric conditions [1]. Regulation varies: a T Nation user notes that in their country products such as yohimbine require a prescription [25].

lore.intro: Yohimbine is described in cutting forums as an add-on for lean bodybuilders targeting stubborn fat, usually with caffeine and fasted cardio [5][16][6].
